t: Al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — The Last Tape
a: المغني المفيد -الشريط الأخير-
b: 'chapter: what has come concerning the covenant of god and the covenant of his prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace.' this chapter was set down for another kind of the oneness of god (tawḥīd), namely right conduct towards god, glorified and exalted — here, in the matter of his covenant (dhimmah): that god's covenant and the covenant of his messenger, may god bless him and grant him peace, are not to be granted. rather, when a commander wishes to conclude a pledge of protection, he grants his own covenant and the covenant of those believers who are with him. the dhimmah is a pledge; it is that for the breaking of which one is blamed — that which, when a person breaks it, he is blamed for it. this is what is called the dhimmah. 'the covenant of god' means his pledge, and 'the covenant of his prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace,' means his pledge — because of his words, exalted is he: {and fulfil the covenant of god when you have made a covenant} (sūrat al-naḥl 16:91),

t: Al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Three
a: المغني المفيد -الشريط الثالث-
b: god, exalted is he, said: 'o son of adam, were you to come to me with the earth's fill of sins...' — 'o son of adam': this is an address to the whole human race. 'were you to come to me with the earth's fill' — that is, with as much as would fill it — 'of sins', that is, of wrongdoings, 'then meet me' — that is, were you to die — 'associating nothing with me' — this is a circumstantial clause, meaning: were you to die free of associating partners with god (shirk), were you to die upon the oneness of god (tawḥīd) — 'i would come to you with the like of it in forgiveness.' 'i would come to you' means: i would requite you; 'with the like of it', that is, with the earth's fill, 'in forgiveness'. what is meant by 'coming' here is presenting oneself before god, glorified and exalted. 'were you to come to me with the earth's fill of sins' — what is meant by it is that when a person dies he will come bearing his record of deeds (ţāʾir) when he is gathered

t: Al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Two
a: المغني المفيد -الشريط الثانى-
b: the fourth lifespan is the lifespan of the gathering upon al-sāhirah: {and a day with your lord is like a thousand years of your counting} (sūrat al-ḥajj 22:47). the fifth lifespan — and it is the last — is the everlasting, unending lifespan, in a garden or in a fire, abiding and remaining forever in them. it is the lifespan of recompense, which follows upon the lifespan of deeds. the lifespan of deeds is the shortest of the lifespans and the lifespan of recompense the longest; and this is part of the bounty of god, glorified and exalted, and part of the completeness of his justice,

t: Al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Fifteen
a: المغني المفيد -الشريط الخامس عشر-
b: 'so when you see what you find hateful' — that is, when you see a wind coming on that you find hateful. gale winds often bring houses down; crops are damaged by them and people are harmed. 'so when you see what you find hateful' — that is, what you expect that from — 'then say: o god, we ask you for the good of this wind, and the good of what is in it, and the good of what it has been commanded with' (اللهم إنا نسألك من خير هذه الريح وخير ما فيها وخير ما أمرت به). these are three supplications. the first supplication is 'o god, we ask you for the good of this wind': the wind itself may bring good and may bring evil,

t: Al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Five
a: المغني المفيد -الشريط الخامس-
b: 'nineteenth: his saying, "i shall certainly give the banner"' — tomorrow — 'to a man who loves god and his messenger and whom god and his messenger love; god will grant victory at his hands' — 'is one of the signs of prophethood', and one of its proofs, because god did grant victory at his hands, so god brought about what his messenger, may god bless him and grant him peace, had announced, and that was an evidentiary miracle (muʿjizah) for the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace. 'twentieth: his spitting into his eyes is likewise one of its signs' — that is, his being cured by the prophet's spittle applied to his eyes is one of the signs of prophethood, and that is a clear proof of his blessedness, may god bless him and grant him peace. 'twenty-first: the merit of ali, may god be pleased with him' — for the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, announced this to the people beforehand, and presented it in a manner calculated to make them eager to compete for it and to attach importance to it ..

t: Al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Four
a: المغني المفيد -الشريط الرابع-
b: 'tenth: the merit of the followers of moses' — because the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, explained that he saw a great throng and supposed them to be his own community, and he was told: this is moses and his community. so this is a merit of the followers of moses, those of the children of israel who believed in him, for god favoured them above the worlds, as he states explicitly in his book; and what is meant by 'the worlds' is those of their own time who belonged to them. 'eleventh: the communities being displayed before him, may god bless him and grant him peace' — that is because he is the witness over this community, which is itself the witness over all the communities, as god, exalted is he, said: {and thus we made you a middlemost community, so that you might be witnesses over the people, and the messenger might be a witness over you} (sūrat al-baqarah 2:143). so the messenger, may god bless him and grant him peace, is the witness over this community, which is the witness over the people; and so the communities are displayed before him for the giving of witness, because a condition (sharţ) of bearing witness is knowledge,

t: Al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Seven
a: المغني المفيد -الشريط السابع-
b: 'second: the explanation of al-tiwalah' — it is what they used to claim makes a man beloved to his wife, or a woman beloved to her husband. like it is everything of that sort, such as the beads that are taken up to make a person beloved to people, as they claim; and there is in it too a kind of sorcery, because in many cases it is taken up in order to extort from people and take their wealth. 'third: that these three are all of them a form of associating partners with god (shirk), without exception.' as for his words 'without exception': the exception has already been made, and he himself stated it plainly when he said, 'and the evidence has singled out from among them whatever is free of shirk.' so what is meant is: whatever among them involves shirk is subject to the prohibition (manhī ʿanhu), without exception,

t: Commentary on al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Nine
a: شرح المغنى المفيد -الشريط التاسع-
b: these innovations in religion (bidʿah) are the side-paths branching off right and left; they are the opened doors with curtains hung over them. whoever enters one of those doors finds it hard to come out of it afterwards, and at every one of those doors there is a devil calling to it and making it seem fair to people. once people hold fast to it and a number of them take it up, it becomes a 'sunnah' in their eyes, and whoever rejects it becomes, in their eyes, one who rejects the sunnah. at that point they take what is wrong (munkar) to be right and what is right (maʿrūf) to be wrong, and they cling to that wrong — even though the revealed laws and sound human nature reject it,

t: Commentary on al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Thirteen
a: شرح المغنى المفيد -الشريط الثالث عشر-
b: 'chapter: on one who denies something of the names and the attributes.' this chapter was set down for another category of what runs counter to the oneness of god (tawḥīd) and conflicts with it, namely the negation of god's oneness in his names and attributes — in the sense that a person denies some of the names or some of the attributes and rejects them, or denies them all. the one who rejects all of that has denied the whole: he has denied god's names and his attributes. the one who rejects the attributes but not the names is likewise, and the one who rejects some of the attributes but not others is likewise,

t: Commentary on al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Eight
a: شرح المغنى المفيد -الشريط الثامن-
b: twelfth: his earnestness, may god bless him and grant him peace, to the point that he did what caused him to be charged with madness. for when there was revealed to him {and warn your nearest kinsfolk} (sūrat al-shuʿarāʾ 26:214), he summoned them all until they had gathered around him at al-safa; and when he told them that he was the naked warner (al-nadhīr al-ʿuryān) and that he was a warner to them of a severe punishment lying ahead of them, abu lahab said to him: 'may you perish — is it for something like this that you gather us?' so god, exalted is he, sent down: {perish the two hands of abu lahab, and perish he. his wealth availed him nothing, nor what he earned.} (sūrat al-masad 111:1–2). and they used to ask him, 'are you mad?' — because they did not understand his call

t: Commentary on al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Twelve
a: شرح المغنى المفيد -الشريط الثاني عشر-
b: and he says: {and they will not cease to fight you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able} (sūrat al-baqarah 2:217). for that reason, whenever the nations of unbelief set upon the muslims together, it only increases the people of faith in faith, in certainty, and in seeking god's reward. and whenever one of their crises comes, people divide into four positions. the first position is the position of the people of faith and certainty, which god set out in sūrat al-ahzab in his words: {and when the believers saw the confederates they said, 'this is what god and his messenger promised us, and god and his messenger spoke truly' — and it only increased them in faith and in submission} (sūrat al-aḥzāb 33:22)

t: Commentary on al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Eleven
a: شرح المغنى المفيد -الشريط الحادي عشر-
b:
'chapter: what has come concerning al-nushrah.' on the authority of jabir: the messenger of god, may god bless him and grant him peace, was asked about al-nushrah and said, 'it is from the work of satan.' narrated by ahmad with a good chain of transmission (sanad jayyid), and by abu dawud, who said: ahmad was asked about it and said, 'ibn masud used to hold all of this disliked (yakrahu).'

al-nushrah is the undoing of sorcery by something resembling sorcery, or by another act of sorcery. the scholars have differed over it. the majority of them held it to be forbidden (taḥrīm) and held it to be a kind of sorcery,

t: Commentary on al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Fourteen
a: شرح المغنى المفيد -الشريط الرابع عشر-
b: this momentous story the messenger of god, may god bless him and grant him peace, related to us in order to draw attention to acknowledging a blessing and binding it fast by giving thanks for it, and to warn against being ungrateful for it and denying it. he explained that there were three men of the children of israel whom god, glorified and exalted, tested: he tested one of them with a skin disease (baraṣ), another with baldness, and another with blindness. then god willed to test them — that is, to put them to the proof — with the trial of ease instead of the trial of hardship; for he had first tested them with the trial of hardship, and then tested them after that with the trial of ease,

t: Commentary on al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape Ten
a: شرح المغنى -المفيد الشريط العاشر -
b: 'and i asked my lord for my community that he not destroy it by a general sanah' — what is meant here by sanah is drought. so no all-encompassing, general drought will overtake it, sweeping over its easts and its wests; rather, when drought strikes one land, fertility strikes another land among the lands of the muslim community. 'and that he not set over them an enemy from outside themselves who would violate their bayḍah' — that is, who would gain mastery over the whole community together. 'and my lord said: o muhammad, when i have decreed a decree, it is not turned back.'

t: Commentary on al-Mughnī al-Mufīd — Tape One
a: شرح المغني المفيد -الشريط الأول-
b:
in the name of god, the most merciful, the ever-merciful. all praise belongs to god, lord of the worlds, and i ask god to bless and grant peace to the one who was sent as a mercy to all the worlds, and to his family, his companions, and all who follow his guidance and keep to his sunnah until the day of judgement.

to proceed: this is kitāb al-tawḥīd alladhī huwa ḥaqq allāh ʿalā al-ʿabīd — 'the book of divine oneness, which is god's right over his servants' — by the erudite scholar shaykh muhammad ibn abd al-wahhab ibn sulayman al-tamimi al-najdi. it sets out the devoting of worship to god alone, glorified and exalted, which is one of the categories of the oneness of god (tawḥīd), together with the connected matters that belong to its completion,

t: Scenes of the Resurrection
a: مشاهد القيامة
b:
all praise belongs to god, lord of the worlds, and i ask god to bless and grant peace to the one who was sent as a mercy to all the worlds, and to his family, his companions, and all who follow his guidance and keep to his sunnah until the day of judgement.

to proceed: a human being is travelling towards a resting place of his own which he will meet without fail, so he must reflect on what lies ahead of him and call to mind those scenes that are waiting for him, because that is what prompts a person to prepare for them. it was for this that the messenger of god, may god bless him and grant him peace, went out with a funeral, and when the dead man had been placed in his grave he looked at his companions and said: 'my brothers, prepare for a lying-down like this one.'

t: Fatwas on Creed
a: فتاوي في العقيدة
b:
affirming certain attributes of god, exalted is he, such as the eye. some of the scholars have affirmed of god an eye, a foot and a leg, and certain other attributes. how correct is this position in the light of the book of god and the sunnah of his messenger, may god bless him and grant him peace?

god, glorified and exalted, is such that {no vision can encompass him, while he encompasses all vision; and he is the all-subtle, the all-aware} (sūrat al-anʿām 6:103); and it is impossible that he should have any like, because of his words, exalted is he: {there is nothing like him, and he is the all-hearing, the all-seeing} (sūrat al-shūrā 42:11). so he cannot be known except by way of what he has told us, and he has told us about himself by these attributes. we therefore believe in them just as god, glorified and exalted, has stated them, and this is obligatory (wājib) upon every muslim. accordingly, he is obliged to believe that they do not resemble the attributes of created beings, and that god, glorified and exalted, has an essence that does not resemble the essences of created beings. just as he has an essence that does not resemble their essences, so too he has attributes that do not resemble their attributes. what is said concerning the attributes is like what is said concerning the essence, and what is said concerning some of the attributes is like what is said concerning others.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

the states of people on the bridge

what are the states of people on the bridge?

on the day of resurrection, when people have been presented and then gathered, they will set out upon the bridge, and they will differ upon it according to their deeds. among them is one who passes like a flash of lightning; among them one who passes like the wind let loose; among them one who passes like the finest of horses and camels; among them one who passes like a man running hard; and among them one who crawls along on his backside. so there is the one saved and delivered whole, the one scratched but let go, and the one flung headlong on his face into the fire of hell. that people should differ upon it by so great a difference entails that some of them will suffer no harm at all from it: they pass like a flash of lightning, feeling no distress and no hardship (mashaqqah) from the bridge.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

the pillars of faith and its branches

the pillars of faith mentioned in the hadith of gabriel — are they all of the pillars of faith? what is the rank of jihad? and what of the hadith of the branches?

as for these pillars, they are the pillars of faith which the messenger of god, may god bless him and grant him peace, set out in the hadith of gabriel; and this is by way of making clear that what is meant by faith is the work of the heart. as for the pillars of islam, they will come to us, god willing, in the next lesson: they are establishing the prayer, giving zakat, fasting ramadan, and pilgrimage to the house for whoever is able to find a way to it. these are what appear in the hadith of ibn umar: 'islam is built upon five — the testimony that there is no god but god and that muhammad is the messenger of god, establishing the prayer, giving zakat, pilgrimage to the house, and fasting ramadan.' as for striving in the path of god (jihad), the messenger, may god bless him and grant him peace, mentioned that it is the summit of the hump of faith, and it has likewise been counted among the pillars of islam, because it is an independent obligation (wājib). all these pillars are independent obligations, and the remaining obligations besides them are among the things that complete them. but this does not make it a pillar (rukn) among the pillars of faith; rather it is a pillar among the pillars of islam, according to the detail given above. as for the hadith of the branches of faith — 'faith is some sixty-odd branches', as it is in sahih al-bukhari, and in sahih muslim 'some seventy-odd branches', 'and modesty is a branch of faith' — what is meant by these branches is the particulars of faith, that is, the particulars of the action that follows from faith; and for that reason modesty was mentioned among them. it also came in it that the highest of them is 'there is no god but god' and the lowest of them is removing what is harmful from the road; all of these are among the branches of faith. just as unbelief too has branches, among which the messenger, may god bless him and grant him peace, mentioned usurious gain (ribā); and he mentioned that ribā is seventy doors, and that the lowest of them is like a man committing fornication with his own mother — we seek refuge with god.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

the use of the jadāwil

i have a father who uses the jadāwil. what should i do about him?

the science of the jadwal, or the science of squaring (al-tarbīʿ), is one of the evil sciences. learning it, teaching it and occupying oneself with it are forbidden (ḥarām) — all of that is forbidden. and if a person is known for using it, that is an impugnment of his standing as a witness: his testimony is not accepted among the muslims. for that reason it is obligatory (wājib) to counsel him. a person is obliged to counsel his father in the best way. and if he is able to steal away the jadāwil that his father has, or to destroy them, in such a way that his father will not become angry with him, that is better for him: he steals them from his books or from his chest, or destroys them, in such a way that the father does not come to know of it.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

whether the marriage bond holds in paradise. on whether the marriage bond holds on the day of resurrection, given the presence of the ḥūr al-ʿīn in paradise?

as for the women of this world, whoever among t

t: Seeking a Means of Nearness (Tawassul)
a: التوسل
b:
question: i submitted a request to one of the shaykhs to be admitted to his sufi order (ṭarīqah), and he granted it to me together with conditions, among them: taking the matter in earnest, keeping the covenant, keeping it secret, not breaching the condition, not breaching the oneness of god (tawḥīd), and not breaching the obligatory duties (farāʾiḍ). i am without knowledge of the sacred sciences. so i remained on that footing, on the path and in the service of the shaykh, until he died. i then grew accustomed to visiting with reverence and with supplication, and after that i seek nearness to god by his righteous deeds, just as i used to seek nearness through him while he was alive, in order to gain benefits and remove harms. is this from the sunnah, or is it associating partners with god (shirk) — may god protect us from it?

answer: these counsels the shaykh gave him are unobjectionable. a person must take the matter in earnest, must fulfil the covenant, must likewise not breach the oneness of god nor the obligatory duties, and must learn sacred knowledge. these are counsels that the shaykh is obliged to give, and the one counselled is obliged to be counselled with them always.

for the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, said: «religion is sincere counsel.» we said: 'to whom?' he said: «to god, to his book, to his messenger, to the leaders of the muslims, and to the generality of them.»

as for what he mentioned about being without knowledge: the mere formulae of remembrance that he performs are no substitute for seeking sacred knowledge. rather, a person is bound to learn what the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, brought — for it may be that what he is doing is in the first place contrary to what the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, brought. so let him search out what the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, brought; let him act by it; and let him make it the judge over everything besides it. if what the shaykh or anyone else ordered agrees with what the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, brought, then let a person act by it, because the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, ordered him to. and if it is contrary to anything the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, brought, then let him throw it back at whoever said it, whoever that may be; and let him not be ashamed to reject from anyone something that contradicts what the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, brought — even if it be a father, or a shaykh, or an elder. it is not possible for you to accept from anyone at all what is contrary to what the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, brought.

as for what this person does after the death of the shaykh mentioned, by way of visiting: visiting graves is recommended (mandūb) in general for muslims, so as to call the hereafter to mind. but the one visited derives no benefit from it, does not perceive it, does not feel it at all, hears nothing of what the visitor says, and cannot benefit him with anything: he does not lift any harm from him nor bring him any benefit, and there is no relation at all between the two. rather you take admonition from his bones, which the earth consumes; you take admonition from his private affairs and his wealth, which have become the property of someone else; and you take admonition from his family, who used to think that he benefited them and saw to their affairs, and he has gone from them and has done them no harm at all. this is what accrues to you from visiting any grave whatsoever. visiting graves — whether those in them are people of faith or people of unbelief, people of uprightness or people of open sin, whether you know them or do not know them — leads to this calling to mind, the calling to mind of the hereafter, and this is what is sought from it. as for the dead, they benefit in their graves only from supplication: that you supplicate for them. and when you supplicate for them, whether you are beside them at their graves or away from them, they do not hear — but they benefit, and there is no difference. the supplication reaches them, whether from near or from far, by night or by day, in whatever place you are.

as for the innovated visitation that people perform — going to the graves, speaking at them, frequenting them, standing over the tombs, and even raising their needs to them — this is without doubt manifest associating of partners with god (shirk). and of this same kind is seeking nearness by the deeds of other persons: this is not lawful for you. what is lawful for you is only to seek nearness by your own deeds, because you are asking god by something that you yourself have put forward; for you cannot seek nearness to him by the deed of another person, since that person is the one entitled to it — for it is the doer who is paid his wage in full. so every person may seek nearness by a deed that he himself has done and in which he was sincere for god; but he can never seek nearness by the deed of another person. so this brother must repent to god for what has passed, must abandon seeking nearness by the deeds of other persons which he did not himself do, must keep to earnestness and to the covenant as he was ordered, and to the oneness of god and the obligatory duties, and must learn sacred knowledge. this is better for him, and this is what adheres to the sunnah of the messenger of god, may god bless him and grant him peace.

(and in general, tawassul belongs properly to jurisprudence (fiqh) and not to the articles of creed.)

t: Fatwas on Creed
a: فتاوي في العقيدة
b:
reconciling the hadith 'god does not take knowledge away by snatching it out' with the statement that the qur'an will be erased from the written copies and from people's breasts on one of the nights. how can one reconcile the hadith 'god does not take knowledge away by snatching it out' with the statement that the qur'an will be erased from the written copies and from people's breasts on one of the nights?

this will only be at the end of time, when knowledge is taken up and ignorance becomes widespread, and the qur'an remains only as a thing to seek blessing by and no longer remains for knowledge. for part of the qur'an's being taken up is that it should remain only as a thing to seek blessing by — so that it remains as charms hung on the insane and the afflicted, or as ornaments with which houses are decorated, while acting by it and judging by it in the daytime is abandoned, and standing in prayer with it at night is abandoned. this is part of its being taken up; and you have witnessed some of that.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

the khatmah for the deceased

is the khatmah for the deceased permissible or not — the one that is called al-salkah?

whether the reward of [reciting] the qur'an reaches the deceased after his death is a point on which the scholars differ. the position (madhhab) of malik and al-shafi'i is that it does not reach him, on the ground that the governing principle is the words of god, exalted is he: {or has he not been told of what is in the scrolls of moses, and of abraham who fulfilled [what he was charged with] — that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another, and that a person shall have nothing but what he has striven for, and that his striving shall be seen, and then he shall be repaid for it with the fullest repayment} (sūrat al-najm 53:36–41). on this principle, this act does not reach him after death. as for abu hanifah and ahmad, they held that it does reach him, by analogical reasoning (qiyās) from the recitation of the qur'an to voluntary charity (ṣadaqah), to hajj, to the lesser pilgrimage (ʿumrah), and to the other kinds of acts of nearness to god. there is agreement that charity and supplication reach [the deceased] with certainty, and everything besides these two falls within the disagreement — because for charity and supplication sound hadiths (ṣaḥīḥ) from the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, are established, and likewise for hajj and ʿumrah sound hadiths are established, whereas for everything other than all of that no explicit text (naṣṣ) has come from the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace. so the disagreement remains: is this among the fixed, quantified matters (al-muqaddarāt), into which analogical reasoning does not enter, or is it not among the fixed matters, so that analogy is possible in it? this is a point of disagreement in legal theory (uṣūl) that cannot be settled. accordingly, those who perform the khatmah following upon the death of the deceased and wish to convey it to him — the more cautious and the better course for them is to give charity on his behalf and to supplicate for him, for that is what reaches him with no disagreement at all.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

the sinking of the earth that will occur in the east, in the west and in the arabian peninsula

what is the sinking of the earth that will occur in the east, in the west and in the arabian peninsula?

the khasf is the earthquake that causes the face of the earth to go down beneath some of its own layers, and this is among the most severe kinds of earthquake. many such sinkings have occurred in the easts and the wests of the earth, but it is not possible to assert with certainty that any one of these sinkings is the one meant in the hadith — even though three sinkings did come close together, one of them in the east, another in the west and another in the arabian peninsula. the one that occurred in the east is the sinking you have heard of in iran; the sinking that occurred in the west is the sinking of the city of al-asnam in algeria; and the sinking in the arabian peninsula is the sinking of the city of dhamar in yemen. but it is not possible to assert with certainty that these are the ones meant in the hadith. rather, these are all of them signs and admonitions, and god, exalted is he, says: {and we do not send the signs except to instil fear (59)} [sūrat al-isrāʾ 17:59]. they are a reminder to god's servants to believe in god, glorified and exalted, alone. but one does not assert with certainty that they are the ones meant by the hadith, because nothing has come that would indicate that specifically.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

taking the formulae of remembrance from one particular shaykh

on making it a condition that the formulae of remembrance (dhikr) be taken from one single, particular shaykh?

the remembrance of god is like the other matters of religion: it is taken from everyone who has narrated it and everyone who has transmitted it, and nowadays it is taken from books as well. so if a person turns to sahih al-bukhari, or sahih muslim, or the muwatta', or to the books of the formulae of remembrance, and takes these formulae from them, that is sufficient. it has no special character over and above what holds for all the rulings.

t: What Reaches the Dead and What Does Not
a: الذي يصل للميت و الذي لا يصله
b:
what is known among us as al-tawfiyah for the dead — that is, reciting sūrat al-ikhlāṣ eleven times on the night before friday and sending its reward to the dead: does it reach them? and is it established in the sunnah or not?

this has not come down in the sunnah from the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace. it is well known that the good is what the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, brought from god, and that whatever he did not bring has no good in it. reciting the qur'an and making a gift of its reward to the dead is a point of disagreement among the scholars. the position of malik and al-shafi'i is that it does not reach them. what is strange is that the people of this country are malikis, and yet we find this custom widespread among them, while malik's position is that it does not reach. malik's position is that the recitation does not reach the dead, and that what does reach them is supplication and voluntary charity (ṣadaqah). mawlud, may god have mercy on him, said: *the reward of food and of supplication, if they are given on the dead man's behalf — there is no disagreement that the two reach him.*

even so, the position of abu hanifah and ibn hanbal is that reciting the qur'an and making a gift of its reward to the deceased does reach him, if the gift precedes the recitation, by analogical reasoning (qiyās) from charity and supplication. this is what they call al-talḥīq, namely that a person says, before he recites: 'o god, make the reward of what i am about to recite and the blessing of what i am about to recite a gift from me, sent down, and a mercy from you, arriving, to so-and-so' — and he names him. this then constitutes a gift of that act to him.

the hanbalis and the hanafis drew this analogy from hajj and the lesser pilgrimage (ʿumrah), for the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, permitted hajj and ʿumrah on behalf of the dead. al-bukhari recorded in the ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of anas ibn malik, may god be pleased with him, that a man of the ansar came to the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, and said: 'my mother has died and did not perform hajj; shall i perform hajj on her behalf?' he said: 'perform hajj on behalf of your mother.' in another narration: 'perform hajj on behalf of your mother, and perform ʿumrah' — and that narration is abu dawud's, in the sunan. likewise in the hadith of the woman of khathʿam, that she said: 'o messenger of god, god's obligation of hajj has come upon my father as a very old man who cannot hold himself up on the mount; shall i perform hajj on his behalf?' he said: 'tell me: if your father owed a debt, would you not have paid it?' she said: 'yes.' he said: 'then discharge what is owed by him, for god's debt has the better right to be discharged.' and the messenger of god, may god bless him and grant him peace, heard a man saying: 'here i am, o god, on behalf of shubrumah.' he said: 'have you performed hajj for yourself?' he said: 'no.' he said: 'then perform hajj for yourself, and then for shubrumah.' and he heard another saying: 'here i am, o god, on behalf of ʿarfaṭah.' he said: 'have you performed hajj for yourself?' he said: 'no.' he said: 'then perform hajj for yourself, and then for ʿarfaṭah.'

this entails the permissibility of performing hajj on behalf of the dead, and on behalf of the living as well, by proxy, when they are unable to make the journey. but the analogy of recitation to hajj is problematic, because hajj contains bodily action, action of the heart, verbal action and financial action, whereas recitation is merely verbal action and action of the heart: there is nothing in it of the action of the rest of the body, and nothing of wealth. its analogy is therefore an analogy drawn where a relevant difference is present. so the stronger view is that it does not reach them.

t: Incantations and Amulets
a: الرقى والتمائم
b:
a woman asks about the folk illness (al-sall al-maṣṣ). she has a ram's horn with a black ḥikmah in it, and with it a tazlūmīt. the horn is put into water and the one afflicted with al-sall drinks it and is cured, by god's leave. as for the tazlūmīt, it is used for a woman whose post-natal period has become obstructed. what is the ruling of the sharia on that, bearing in mind that she uses it for the benefit of muslims and knows that it neither harms nor benefits except by god's leave?

these incantations (ruqā) are old, and were part of the business of the age of ignorance. the prophet, upon whom be peace, said: 'present your incantations to me.' whatever in them contained the magnification of god and remembrance of him, the prophet, upon whom be peace, confirmed; and whatever was otherwise, he rejected and forbade. so everything whose meaning a person does not know, it is not lawful for him to use as an incantation.

as for these physical objects — such as horns, and what is called the tazlūmīt, and the like — it is not lawful to use them, because a person does not know what is in them; and if he does know, they are things whose outward appearance is like the outward appearance of sorcery, because they are physical objects and matters of that sort. this kind of thing therefore harms and does not benefit. and whatever immediate benefit is observed from it, such as recovery from one illness or another, is only a trial, because a person will become attached to it and suppose that it heals or benefits. it is a trial by which god tries people.

we are now awaiting the dajjal, so we must be on our guard against things of this kind. if a person is to be on his guard against the trial of the false messiah, let him know that the dajjal brings the dead to life: he calls them and they rise from their graves; he passes by the ruined village and its treasures follow him like swarms of bees; he comes to the people of a village who are in drought and in the utmost distress, and they believe him, so he commands the sky and it rains, and commands the earth and it brings forth growth, and their livestock come home to them in the evening with their udders fuller than they have ever been; and he passes by the people of a village who are in plenty, and they call him a liar, so he commands the sky and it withholds, and commands the earth and it goes barren, and their livestock come home to them in the evening in the worst hardship they have ever known.

so when we know this, and know that these worldly things that are seen are only trials that god, exalted, brings about — just as he brings about what is far graver than them at the hand of the false messiah — then a person must not be deceived by them, and must know that trials exist. a person's following them without examination, and his testimony that the matter is simply something observed — that so-and-so drank this and recovered, and it was hung on such-and-such a woman and she recovered — this kind of thing is only one of the trials a person must be on his guard against; for if everyone who cures a sick person were to be followed, the dajjal would have the better claim to that, since he brings the dead to life. hence the utmost caution is required against this kind of thing, and against its danger to creed, which affects what people believe.

and let us know that god, glorified and exalted, has given us that in which there is healing and light, and has sent down upon us this clear qur'an, which falsehood does not approach from before it or from behind it, a revelation from one all-wise, praiseworthy. it is god's firm rope and his straight path: whoever holds fast to it is preserved, and whoever abandons it — any tyrant who does so — god breaks his back. god, exalted, has said: {and we send down of the qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers} (sūrat al-isrāʾ 17:82). and he said: {and when you recite the qur'an, we place between you and those who do not believe in the hereafter a concealed veil; and we have placed coverings over their hearts, lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness. and when you mention your lord alone in the qur'an, they turn their backs in aversion} (sūrat al-isrāʾ 17:45–46). and he, exalted, said: {and if there were a qur'an by which the mountains were moved, or the earth were cloven apart, or the dead were spoken to — rather, to god belongs the affair entirely} (sūrat al-raʿd 13:31). so we must content ourselves with the book of god, exalted, and seek guidance in it, and beware of these preoccupations that divert us from it.

t: The Difference Between islām and īmān
a: الفرق بين الإسلام والإيمان
b:
the messenger of god, upon whom be peace, explained faith (īmān) in the hadith of the delegation of ʿabd al-qays with the very thing by which he explained submission (islām) in the hadith of gabriel. how are the two explanations to be reconciled?

faith (īmān) and submission (islām) are two terms of the revealed law: when they are brought together they part, and when they are parted they come together. if they occur within a single context, their meanings differ, as in the hadith of gabriel; and if they occur in two different contexts, their meaning is one, as in the hadith of the delegation of ʿabd al-qays.

as for the hadith of the delegation of ʿabd al-qays: when they said to the messenger of god, upon whom be peace, 'we cannot reach you except in the sacred month, and between us and you is this clan of the unbelievers of mudar, so command us with a decisive command which we may act upon and may pass on to those we have left behind, and by which we may enter the garden' — he commanded them four things and forbade them four. he said: 'i command you to believe in god alone. do you know what belief in god alone is?' and he explained belief in god alone to them as: that they bear witness that there is no god but god and that muhammad is the messenger of god, that they establish the prayer, and that they render a fifth of the spoils. and he set out for them the four things they were to abandon, among the drinks. so he explained the concept of īmān to them by part of the concept of islām — which shows that when īmān and islām occur singly, their meaning is one.

as for when they occur within a single context — like the verse of sūrat al-ḥujurāt, god's words, exalted is he: {the bedouins said: we have believed. say: you have not believed; rather say: we have submitted} (sūrat al-ḥujurāt 49:14) — then their meanings differ, as in the hadith of gabriel. so too the hadith of saʿd ibn abi waqqas in the two ṣaḥīḥs: that the messenger of god, upon whom be peace, gave to a number of men and left out one man, who was the most pleasing of them to me; and what i knew of him overcame me, so i said: 'o messenger of god, what is it with you and so-and-so? by god, i consider him a believer.' he said: 'or a muslim.' so the messenger, upon whom be peace, distinguished between the two words when they occurred within a single context.

t: Various Fatwas
a: فتاوي متنوعة
b:
the difference between the soul (nafs) and the spirit (rūḥ)

what is the difference between the soul (nafs) and the spirit (rūḥ)?

this is a point of disagreement among the scholars. the stronger view is that 'spirit' is applied to the power by which there is life, and that 'soul' is applied to the inward dimension of the human being. so the soul is what is called, for example, the heart, while the spirit takes in all the inward faculties, so that the soul, the heart, the intellect, discernment and the rest fall under it. for this reason animals have spirits, which are taken at death, but they do not have those faculties — they have no intellect, for instance; that belongs to the human being alone.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

the difference between ahl al-sunnah and al-jamāʿah

ahl al-sunnah wa-l-jamāʿah — what is the difference between the two?

this is a technical term which has not come down in the book or in the sunnah. what came were hadiths containing the command to [hold to] the sunnah, and hadiths containing the command to [hold to] the congregation (jamāʿah). it is established from the messenger of god, upon whom be peace, in his counsel narrated from him by al-irbad ibn sariyah, may god be pleased with him, that he said: 'whoever of you lives will see much disagreement, so you must keep to my sunnah and to the sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs; bite onto it with your back teeth.' this is a command from him to follow the sunnah. likewise there came from the prophet, upon whom be peace, the urging to hold to his sunnah in many hadiths, such as the hadith of al-miqdam ibn madikarib, may god be pleased with him, that the messenger of god, upon whom be peace, said: 'is it not near that a man, full-fed, reclining on his couch, to whom there comes a matter of my command — of what i have commanded or what i have forbidden — will say: between us and you is the book of god; whatever we find in it of the lawful we hold lawful, and whatever we find in it of the forbidden we hold forbidden. truly, what the messenger of god has forbidden is like what god has forbidden. truly, i have been given the qur'an and the like of it along with it.'

likewise there came from him, upon whom be peace, the urging to [hold to] the congregation in many hadiths, such as his words to hudhayfah ibn al-yaman: 'keep to the congregation of the muslims and their leader'; and his words, upon whom be peace: 'the blood of a muslim is not lawful except for one of three: the previously married person who commits adultery, a life for a life, and the one who abandons his religion and separates from the congregation'; and his words, upon whom be peace: 'whoever separates from the congregation by a handspan dies the death of the age of ignorance'; and his words, upon whom be peace: 'whoever separates from the congregation has cast the yoke of islam from his neck'; and his words, upon whom be peace: 'the hand of god is with the congregation, and whoever breaks away, breaks away into the fire'; and his words, upon whom be peace: 'whoever desires the very heart of the garden, let him keep to the congregation'; and his words, upon whom be peace: 'the hand of god is over the congregation, and the wolf eats only the sheep that has strayed far off'; and likewise his prohibition of reverting to desert life after the emigration. the hadiths in this chapter are many.

so these hadiths taken all together — the first set, indicating adherence to the sunnah, and the second set, indicating adherence to the congregation — the scholars joined the two and made the white, clear road which the prophet, upon whom be peace, and his companions were upon 'the sunnah and the congregation'. what is meant by 'the sunnah' here is therefore not merely what is called sunnah in the jurists' usage — that is, the status of a legally commanded act which is commanded in a non-binding way, such that the one who performs it is rewarded and the one who omits it is not punished. that is the sunnah of the jurists and the legal theorists, and it is not what is intended here. likewise, what is meant by 'the congregation' is not simply the numerous individuals and the great mass; rather, god, exalted, says: {and if you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the path of god} [al-anʿām 116] (sūrat al-anʿām 6:116). what is meant is what the messenger, upon whom be peace, and his companions were upon. this we call 'sunnah and congregation' only as a technical term, and there is no quarrelling over technical terms.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

the difference between the charisms of god's friends and other [extraordinary events]

there are breaks in the customary order, some of which are a charism (karāmah) from god, glorified and exalted, to his friends, and some of which are satanic. how do we distinguish between them?

the distinction is drawn only by the state of the person himself. whoever is committed to the revealed law, conforming in his outward and his inward to the law of god — then what he attains of that is a charism with which god has honoured him. and whoever is at variance with the law, disobedient and an innovator — then what he attains of that is from the side of satan, or is an affliction and a test from god, exalted.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

the view that the fire will pass away

t: On Obsessive Whispering in Purification and Prayer, and How to Treat It
a: الكلام على الوسوسة في الطهارة والصلاة وطرق علاجها
b:
i have a son who is seized by obsessive whispering (waswasah) in purification (ṭahārah) and prayer. when he goes to the lavatory and cleans himself of urine, he performs ablution right through to the end, and then says: i have not got free of the urine, and i cannot pray with substantive impurity (najāsah) on me — and he takes off all his clothing, takes other clothing, and prays.

this kind of thing is from the work of satan. god, exalted, has said: {o you who believe, do not follow the footsteps of satan} (sūrat al-nūr 24:21). so he must treat himself for this illness with the means of healing given in the revealed law. among them: frequent seeking of forgiveness. among them likewise: the remembrances for entering the lavatory and for leaving it, and keeping to them. among them also: not wearying himself by thinking much about this matter — he is obliged to turn it away from himself. among them also: the lawful incantation (ruqyah), that he recite the qur'an over himself and that someone else recite it over him. among them: keeping to the remembrances for sleeping and waking, and for morning and evening. and among them: the voluntary charity (ṣadaqah) by which illness is treated — 'treat your sick with charity.' all of that will remove this obsessive whispering from him, by god's leave.

t: On Breaks in the Customary Order
a: الكلام على خوارق العادات
b:
what appears of extraordinary events at the hand of the friend of god, and what appears at the hand of the sorcerer — what is the difference between them?

the scholars have mentioned that breaks in the customary order are of seven kinds: four of them for good and three of them for evil.

the four that are for good are, first, the precursors (irhāṣāt) that appear at the birth of the prophets and in their childhood — such as the cracking of the arch of chosroes, the dying down of the fire of the persians, what halimah witnessed of extraordinary things in the childhood of the prophet, upon whom be peace, the opening of his breast, and the like. these are not miracles (muʿjizāt) but precursors; they point to his being sent, since at that time he had not yet been sent — he was sent at the completion of forty years.

the second kind is the miracles: what appears at the hand of the prophets at the point of challenge, in conveying the messages of their lord — such as the descent of revelation, the ascension and the night journey, the splitting of the moon and the like, and such as the she-camel of salih and the staff of moses. this is the miracle, and it belongs to the prophets alone.

the third kind is what is called the charisms of the friends of god (karāmāt al-awliyāʾ): what god honours with it whoever is of the people of obedience, god-consciousness (taqwā) and faith, from among the things that help him toward obedience — such as bodily strength, so that a person is able to keep up ablution and full washing; this is a charism with which god honours his friends. of the same kind is keeping to the first row, or to answering the one who calls to prayer, or to praying in congregation, or to completing the qur'an every day and night, for example, or keeping to the night prayer through the whole year. this is a charism with which god honours whom he wills of his friends, and it is a break with the custom of most people. this kind is called the charisms, and most of them are not directed toward this world but toward the affairs of the hereafter. charisms are in most cases not directed toward worldly matters, such as a person finding money or a car or a telephone or the like; those are trivial worldly matters, whereas god's honouring of his servants is bound up with matters greater than this — as when he honours his friends with what helps them toward his worship and his obedience, and with what increases them in faith, awe and god-consciousness.

the fourth kind is what is called assistance (ʿawn): what is attained by the middling sort of muslims, who are not renowned for obedience or for worship, so that god ordains for such a person something that breaks the customary order on account of his faith — like one whose mount bolted from him in an empty tract of land and a tree held it back for him. this kind is among what gives help in worldly matters; it does not fall within the scope of the charism, but is of the assistance by which god assists his servants, ordaining for them what helps them in their worldly affairs, of what breaks the customary order.

these are the four for good. as for the three that are for evil: the first is what is called humiliation (ihānah), namely the extraordinary events that appear at the hand of a false claimant to messengerhood, contrary to his claim. musaylimah the liar heard that the prophet, upon whom be peace, had wiped the head of a boy and that the boy did not go grey — his hair stayed black until he died an old man. so musaylimah wiped the head of a boy, and the boy went bald. and he heard that the prophet, upon whom be peace, spat into a well that was salt and it became sweet; so he spat into a well and it dried up. this kind is called humiliation: it is in fact a break in the customary order — this is a break in the customary order, but it is a humiliation, because it is not in the manner sought, and is the opposite of the manner the person seeks.

the second kind of these breaks that are for evil is sorcery (siḥr). sorcery is what has already been defined, in its two kinds: what is illusion, and what is actual effect. by it a break in the customary order comes about, and it is for evil; it is unbelief on the part of the one who does it.

the third kind of the breaks that are for evil is what is called soothsaying (kihānah) and consorting with the jinn. the jinn break the customary order for the human being: they hear a single word from the unseen and add to it ninety-nine lies, so they bring him a hundred words, among which is one word of truth and ninety-nine lies. then he reports what they have reported to him, so that at one time a truthful one comes to him and at another a lying one — as saf ibn sayyad said to the messenger of god, upon whom be peace, when he asked him, as is in the ṣaḥīḥ. he said: 'what comes to you, saf?' he said: 'a truthful one and a lying one come to me.' he said: 'be off with you; you will never go beyond your measure.' so the prophet, upon whom be peace, knew that what comes to him is from satan, because what is from god has no liar in it — it must be truthful. so he said, 'a truthful one and a lying one come to me', and he said: 'be off with you; you will never go beyond your measure.'

these, then, are the breaks in the customary order. their divisions are clear and the distinction between them is plain. what causes difficulty for some people is only what happens to some of the friends of god: that they report certain things of the unseen, being people of uprightness and righteousness, and at times they are right in that and at times they are wrong. the answer to this is that they are obliged not to report what they have come upon of that; it is forbidden (ḥarām) for them to report it. and if they do report some of it and it turns out true, the people of faith must not be taken in by it, and must know that this happens to the righteous and to the corrupt, and happens to the believer and to others.

that is why imam al-junayd, m

t: Fatwas on Creed
a: فتاوي في العقيدة
b:
obsessive whispering concerning creed

what is the ruling concerning one who is exposed to satan's obsessive whisperings in his creed? what is he advised to do?

when a person senses anything of satan's whispering in what he believes, he must know that this is one of the footsteps of satan, which god, exalted, has forbidden us to follow, for god, exalted, has said: {o you who believe, do not follow the footsteps of satan} (sūrat al-nūr 24:21). he must make much remembrance of god, exalted, for that drives satan away. so let him make much seeking of forgiveness, and let him say 'there is no god but god', for this cuts off satan's path and removes those whisperings entirely. and he must not pursue the thought: if a passing thought comes, he must not turn it over again, but should cut it off with the remembrance of god, exalted...

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

by what are creed and the foundations of religion established?

are creed and the foundations of religion established by a singly transmitted report (khabar al-āḥād)?

the singly transmitted report is of four types in the usage of the hadith scholars. the first of them is the widespread (mustafīḍ), which comes close to the mass-transmitted (mutawātir); separating the two is laborious. by this, creedal doctrines are established without disagreement. the second is the well-known (mashhūr), which is what a number narrated in every layer, not exceeding ten and not falling below three or four. next to it is the strong (ʿazīz), which is what two or three alone narrated in one of the layers. next to it is the singular (gharīb), which is what one narrator alone narrated in one layer, in whichever of its layers that may be.

over these three, people differed as to whether they yield certainty or not. the majority of the legal theorists held that a singly transmitted report, whether well-known, strong or singular, does not yield certainty. the verifying scholars among them held that it does yield certainty if it is attended by indications that point to it. others held that it yields certainty absolutely, and this is narrated from the majority of the hadith scholars. but the correct position is that singly transmitted reports, if they are attended by indications, do yield certainty; and the hadith scholars give as their example of this what malik narrates from nafi from ibn umar from the messenger of god, upon whom be peace, for it yields certainty on account of the indications attending it.

on this disagreement, they differed over taking singly transmitted reports as evidence in creedal doctrines. creedal doctrines divide into two kinds: what certainty is required in, namely the foundations of the creeds and of the religions; and what certainty is not required in, namely their details — such as the details of the attributes of god, glorified and exalted, and the like. the details of the attributes, on the stronger view, do not have certainty as a condition, and therefore singly transmitted reports are accepted in them. so it is possible for an attribute to be established for god, mighty and majestic, by a singly transmitted report, and it is possible for a name to be established for him by that.

that is why al-suyuti, may god have mercy on him, says: *his names, glorified be he, are fixed by revelation; a third position holds it of the name only, not of the attribute. and a single instance suffices, and the verbal noun, and the verb, and the suppositions, in the view of the one whose opinion counts.* 'the suppositions' means singly transmitted reports.

as for matters of certainty, and the foundations — the foundations of the religions — certainty is indispensable in them. so on the view that a singly transmitted report yields certainty absolutely, there is no difficulty in their being established by it. and on the view that it yields certainty if attended by indications, the same holds — as with what al-bukhari narrated in the ṣaḥīḥ, or what muslim narrated in the ṣaḥīḥ: even if it were singular or strong, there attend it such indications as require certainty about it. and if certainty is stipulated in them, then a singly transmitted report is not taken in them.

our ruling of soundness on what is in the two ṣaḥīḥs is not intended as certainty in the view of the legal theorists; it is intended as certainty only in the view of the hadith scholars. that is why al-iraqi, may god have mercy on him, said in the alfiyyah on hadith terminology: *by 'sound' and 'weak' they intended [a judgement] on the outward, not certainty; and what is relied upon is our refraining from ruling of any chain that it is the soundest absolutely. some people have ventured upon it, and it was said: malik, from nafi, the client of the devout one, in what the latter narrated. and choose, where it is given with a chain from him, al-shafi'i; i said: and from him, ahmad.*

t: Defining the People of Kalām
a: تعريف أهل الكلام
b:
who are the people of kalām, and what do you mean by them?

'the people of kalām' is a name that has become well known as applied to a group of this community who laid down rules for the standards that govern the intellect. that is because the lawgiver referred knowledge of some matters to the intellect, while people's understandings are disparate and divergent, and it is not possible to make any one of them a proof against the rest. so there was a need to lay down criteria and controls to which people could refer when their intellects diverge.

you know that god's distribution of intellects among people is uneven. that is why the sages say: there is no one who is not content with god as regards his own intellect, and those with the least intellect are the most content with it. the person with the smallest share of intellect thinks he is the most intelligent of people — and this is part of god's wisdom, exalted, and his kindness. so how can judgement be referred to this intellect, in which people vary? controls must be laid down to which reference can be made.

these controls are what are called the proofs and the demonstrations, and the propositions, which are the claims. their basis is the distinction between assent (taṣdīq) and conception (taṣawwur): conception is the grasping of a single notion, and assent is the grasping of a relation — that is, the affirming of one thing of another, or the denying of it.

these rational rules are pure exercise of reasoning; they cannot be a hundred per cent wrong, nor a hundred per cent right. error has occurred in many of their aspects, and especially when the theories of the greeks and the theories of the romans were translated into them; and there is no doubt that the theories of these earlier nations are mixed with much that is pagan and much that associates partners with god.

likewise, many of those who studied the science of kalām and went deep into these rules went to excess concerning the intellect, until they took it out of its proper bounds. the intellect is one of the faculties of the human being; it is like his eye, his ear and his hand, and there can be no going to excess in it, because it has limits at the upper end and limits at the lower end. its limits at the lower end are the primary truths, the observed, the intuited, the sensed and the widely held — these are the lower bound of the intellect. its upper ceiling is the nine points at which intellects come to a halt, which are gathered in the phrase 'ʿajil wa-qatab': the ʿayn is for the absence of both contradictories; the jīm is for joining the two together; the lām is for the necessity of circularity or of infinite regress; the wāw is for the occurrence of a number without end; the qāf is for the reversal of a reality; the tāʾ is for the multiplicity of the agent, and for the obtaining of what already obtains, and likewise for preponderance without a preponderating factor; and the bāʾ is for the collapse of an exhaustive division.

these are nine: they are the points at which intellects come to a halt. and if intellects are like this, then we cannot go to excess concerning them, nor make them the thing to which judgement is referred in all matters. rather, the ruling upon a person is god's address, not the address of the intellect.

from here, many of the theologians err in how they conceive the intellect. that is why al-ghazali, may god have mercy on him, said: revelation is an intellect from without, and the intellect is a revelation from within. there is no doubt that this is part of going to excess concerning the intellect, because the intellect al-ghazali is speaking of is not embodied in the intellect of any particular person — he does not mean the intellect of abu hamid al-ghazali, for instance, or the intellect of a particular human being; rather he means absolute existence, which is the mental existence of the intellect, and he does not mean external existence, embodied in the intellect of one person among persons or one group among groups. and when a judgement is passed on a mental quiddity rather than an external one, it is not a precise judgement.

likewise, part of what has become mixed into what is called the science of kalām is plunging into the attributes of god, exalted, without knowledge — and this is an obliterating danger, because god, exalted: {vision does not grasp him, and he grasps vision; and he is the subtle, the aware (103)} [الأنعام] (sūrat al-anʿām 6:103). we mentioned in the previous lesson that nothing can be affirmed of him except what he has affirmed of himself, or what his messenger, upon whom be peace, affirmed of him; so the knowledge of an originated being cannot reach him — indeed nothing can be known about him except what he has revealed. and if the matter is so, then there is no scope for the intellect in this chapter.

the people of kalām are many groups, and they entered a number of sciences. in the language sciences there is a theologising faction, the one called the people of rational rule-making, and they are the people of kufa. the people of kufa, for instance, when they find any rare linguistic form, draw an analogy upon it and make it a rule; whereas the people of basra lay down a rule by the majority usage, and whatever contradicts it they treat as anomalous, or else they seek an interpretation of it that returns it to the original rule. an example is their disagreement over whether the agent may precede. the people of basra say the agent does not precede: *and after a verb comes an agent; if it appears, that is it, and otherwise a pronoun lies concealed.* but the kufans say no, a preceding agent does exist; and the basrans say that where such a thing is found, it is the agent of an omitted verb indicated by what comes after it.

likewise in legal theory (uṣūl al-fiqh). in legal theory there is a school called the theological school, which builds the principles of legal theory, and the rules of derivation and of drawing on the tex

t: The Reality of Unveiling
a: حقيقة الكشف
b:
what is the reality of unveiling (kashf), and to whom does it occur?

unveiling means that god, exalted, unveils to some of his servants something of the relative unseen. the unseen is of two kinds. there is a real unseen, and this is not unveiled to anyone, because it is of god's knowledge which he has kept to himself, as god, exalted, said: {and with him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but he} [الأنعام 59] (sūrat al-anʿām 6:59). and the prophet, upon whom be peace, said, concerning five which none knows but god: {indeed, god — with him is knowledge of the hour; and he sends down the rain; and he knows what is in the wombs. and no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die} [لقمان 34] (sūrat luqmān 31:34). this real unseen — no created being has any access to it, and it is among the exclusive properties of the deity, majestic is his majesty.

the second kind is the relative unseen: that which some servants come to know and others do not. coming to know it by the accustomed means is not a break with the customary order — as with a physician's coming to know the state of the foetus in its mother's belly, that it is alive and breathing, or that it is male or female, or the like, by means of imaging. this is coming to know by ordinary things; just as when a sheep is slaughtered and skinned and its belly is opened and there is a foetus in it: before it was uncovered it was a relative unseen, and after it was uncovered it became part of the world of the witnessed. this is of the kind of the relative unseen.

likewise, whoever is behind this wall now is not seen by the one on the other side of it; but this unseen is a relative unseen, because if he comes in through the door he sees them, and what had been hidden from him is unveiled to him. and likewise what occurs by means of devices, such as speaking by telephone with a distant person, or seeing him by means of satellites, or by video telephone. this is of the relative unseen, and its discovery in that case, by the accustomed means, is not a break with the customary order.

but its being unveiled by a break with the customary order, with no means at all that we can see — this is unveiling in the sense of a break with the customary order: that a person sees what others do not see in ordinary matters. for instance, if a person looks through a magnifying glass and sees a crescent moon or a distant star, that is not a break with the customary order, because a relative unseen was unveiled to him by an instrument and a means; but if he sees it without an instrument, then that is a break with the customary order, and it is an unveiling of that relative unseen.

this unveiling may be a charism with which god honours some of his friends, disclosing to them certain matters that increase them in faith and in awe of god, and in greater reliance upon him and love for him. and it may be a trial, as god tries with it some of the deluded, disclosing to them some of the relative unseen, so that they take themselves to be disposing of the universe, or to be exercising an influence that is not theirs, and so make false and lying claims. this is a trial upon them.

the like of this happens to the believer and to the unbeliever. this unveiling happens to believers, and happens to unbelievers, and happens to one who makes no claim to islam at all: many of the christians and the jews have this kind of unveiling happen to them. and the greatest of it as a trial upon the people of the earth is what happens of it to the false messiah.

for the false messiah has the most astonishing unveilings happen to him. he shows a person his father and his mother, who died some time ago, and lets him hear their speech. he passes by the ruined village and its treasures follow him like swarms of bees. he comes to the people of a village who are in drought and they believe him, so he commands the sky and it rains, and commands the earth and it brings forth growth, and their livestock come home to them in the evening with their udders fuller than they have ever been. and he passes by the people of a village who are in plenty and they call him a liar, so he commands the sky and it withholds, and commands the earth and it is stripped bare, and their livestock come home to them in the severest hardship. this is of the unveilings that happen to the false messiah.

by this it is known that unveiling is not one of the signs of friendship with god — that it happens to believers and happens to unbelievers, and happens to the enemies of god and happens to the friends of god, each according to what god gives him of it. what happens of it to the friends of god is what increases them in faith, in reliance upon god and in love for him; this is what constitutes a charism. as for what is not like that — such as what increases a person in overweening insolence, and his claiming that he disposes of the universe — this is not a praiseworthy unveiling, and is not a charism.

t: Various Fatwas
a: فتاوي متنوعة
b:
the ruling on enjoining right and forbidding wrong where a woman is concerned

is it permissible for a woman to enjoin right and forbid wrong?

yes; rather she is obliged to enjoin right and forbid wrong. and it is likewise obligatory that right be enjoined upon her: it is obligatory upon men, if they see a wrong among the women, to forbid the wrong and to enjoin the right. the messenger of god, upon whom be peace, used to undertake that himself. in the two ṣaḥīḥs: he delivered the eid sermon, and thought that the women had not heard him, so he leaned upon bilal and stood over the women and admonished them, and said: 'o company of women, give charity, for i have seen you to be the majority of the people of the fire.' so the women wept, and bilal spread out his garment, and the women began reaching with their hands to their jewellery and throwing it into bilal's garment.

------------------------------------------------------------

the ruling on certain remembrances not transmitted from the messenger of god ﷺ and tied to particular occasions

here is a sheet with remembrances written on it, distributed as photocopies, and on it is that this is the glorification for the month of ramadan, and that on the first day one says, a hundred times: 'glory be to the one whom the heavens glorify with their farthest reaches.'

this kind of thing is innovation (bidʿah), and is among what god has not given leave for and what the messenger of god, upon whom be peace, did not bring. for that reason it must be abandoned and left, and in what the messenger of god, upon whom be peace, brought there is sufficiency to dispense with the like of this...

------------------------------------------------------------

the ruling on hanging amulets

is the one who hangs an amulet an associator of partners with god?

this is lesser association (shirk aṣghar), not greater association — unless he believes that it benefits him and lifts harm from him, in which case that is greater association, by virtue of the belief. but merely hanging it is lesser association, which does not take one out of the religion, like swearing by other than god and the like. for the prophet, upon whom be peace, said: 'whoever hangs an amulet is consigned to it'; and he said: 'whoever hangs an amulet — may god not bring anything to completion for him'; and he said: 'whoever hangs anything is consigned to it'; and he likewise said: 'incantations, amulets and love-charms are association.' what is meant by that is an association below association, and it does not take one out of the religion.

------------------------------------------------------------

the ruling on al-kazānah

what is the ruling on what is called al-kazānah, of whatever kind it may be?

god has kept the unseen to himself. he said: {knower of the unseen; and he does not disclose his unseen to anyone} (sūrat al-jinn 72:26). and he said: {say: none in the heavens or the earth knows the unseen except god} (sūrat al-naml 27:65). the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, made clear that the keys of the unseen — which are the locks of the unseen — are five, which none knows but god. and god, exalted, says: {and with him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but he} (sūrat al-anʿām 6:59). and these five are: {indeed, god — with him is knowledge of the hour; and he sends down the rain; and he knows what is in the wombs. and no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die} (sūrat luqmān 31:34).

attempting to look into them — as when a person wants to know his appointed term, or his provision and what he will be provided with tomorrow, or the time the rain will fall, or the coming of one who is absent, or the like — this is among the grave sins. its perpetrator may well be struck with trials; we ask god for safety and well-being. very often the one who seeks to look into that becomes exposed to trials, so that the jinn are set upon him and he is tried in his religion. trial in one's religion is the worst of afflictions; the worst of calamities is calamity in religion. the one who is tried in his religion has some truth appear to him in what the jinn tell him, or in what he comes to know by these means, and so he is put to trial by it and supposes that everything he is told from that quarter is true; and so he follows that dark path, and by it a foot slips after being firm, and he strays from the evenness of the way — we ask god for safety and well-being.

the believer is obliged to submit to god's decree, its good and its evil, and to believe in that; and to know that what has befallen him could not have missed him and what has missed him could not have befallen him; and that the pens have been lifted and the pages have dried over what is to be; and that nothing occurs in the universe except by god's command and his ordering. then he is content with everything that has been written for him, and is not one who reaches after what has been veiled from him. the more firmly bound a person is to god, and the stronger his faith in him, the less he cares to search out things of the unseen and matters he is not given to know.

i know a great old scholar, shaykh muhammad yabra ould bayyah, god's mercy be upon him, who was deaf and could not hear; whoever spoke with him would write for him in the air, and he would understand by the writing. i wrote to him that there is a device placed on the ear by means of which hearing is possible, and that i was ready to provide it for him. he said: i do not wish to come to know what my lord has kept from me. he never consented to use this device, even though it is among the permissible things and is not a matter of seeking to look into things of the unseen; but among the scholars there are those who reach a level of reliance upon god, glorified and exalted, at which they hold this kind of treatment to be like cauterisation — and the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, said: 'i do not like to be c

t: The Expression 'I Guarantee upon God'
a: عبارة أضمن على الله
b:
people have grown accustomed to saying, 'i guarantee upon god that you will have such-and-such.' is this expression acceptable in the revealed law?

this expression rests, in origin, upon a fabricated hadith (mawḍūʿ), in which it comes: 'the miser is the one who does not guarantee upon god.' but this is not sound from the prophet, upon whom be peace; it is among the fabrications. for that reason a person should not say it — unless what he means by it is that the one who does the deed, if he does it seeking god's good pleasure, has been promised good by god for that deed. that is the intention that would make it acceptable; for you are able to guarantee what god has guaranteed in his book. everything that god has undertaken in his book, or that his messenger, upon whom be peace, has undertaken, you know will come to pass — so you can guarantee that it will occur.

t: The Relation of the Science of Logic to the Affirmation of God's Oneness
a: علاقة علم المنطق بالتوحيد
b:
what is the relation of the science of logic to the affirmation of god's oneness (tawḥīd)?

the science of logic is the science of the rational measures by which a person grasps rational proofs. logic comes back to the distinction between conception (taṣawwur) and assent (taṣdīq). conception is the grasp of single terms; assent is the grasp of the relations between them. conception is arrived at only by way of definitions (muʿarrifāt), and assent only by way of proofs (ḥujaj). when a person knows these matters, he knows what counts as a proof rationally, what stands in need of demonstration and what does not; and he knows where error enters into proofs, and how proofs are put together. so it is an instrument of measurement in which there is nothing objectionable in the revealed law, neither in tawḥīd nor in anything else — but it can be turned to good use and it can be turned to evil use. learning it is like learning mathematics, like learning arithmetic, like learning writing: it is one of those measures with which clarified butter may be measured out, and wine may be measured out, and milk may be measured out. it goes according to the use that is made of it.

t: Love of the Messenger of God, Peace and Blessings Be upon Him, and Love of What He Brought
a: محبة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ومحبة ما جاء به
b:
by what means does a person come to love the messenger of god, peace and blessings be upon him, with a complete love, and to love everything he brought?
